RAPID SITUATION ASSESSMENT · NEPAL · UPDATED 27 AUG 2026

Bhote Koshi Flood — Population & Connectivity Assessment

A same-day cross-read of Meta Data for Good crisis signals (population, network, movement) against the Copernicus EMSR927 rapid mapping activation and the ReliefWeb/DFS situation overview, for the 26 August 2026 glacial-lake-outburst flood on the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system.

Meta POP · NET · MOV, 26 Aug 2026 Copernicus EMS EMSR927 ReliefWeb / Data Friendly Space, 27 Aug 2026 Analyst: situational triage, not verified ground truth

What happened

Trigger → path → downstream effects

On 26 August, an ice-and-rock avalanche is believed to have blocked the Lhende Khola — a Bhote Koshi tributary on the Nepal–China border — forming a debris-dammed lake roughly 20 km upstream of the Miteri Bridge that then burst. The USGS initially logged a M4.4 earthquake at 08:37 local time, then revised it to a M5.2 glacial collapse. The surge travelled roughly 60 km down the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani systems in under a day.

Population variance: crisis vs. baseline

Meta POP · z-score by tile, latest snapshot (16:00 NPT)

Each dot is an ~800 m Meta population tile, colored by how far its 26 Aug reading sits from its own baseline (z-score, capped at ±4). Red = fewer detected people/devices than expected; teal = more, plotted over OpenTopoMap terrain so the corridor's relief is visible under the signal. Dashed outlines mark the approximate rapid-triage zones used throughout this page — bounding boxes, not administrative boundaries.

Network conditions in the impact zone

Meta NET · pre-event coverage footprint, 00:00 NPT 26 Aug

This NET snapshot was captured roughly nine hours before the flood's ~09:00 onset — it is a baseline connectivity-infrastructure footprint, not a live post-disaster outage feed. Every tile the product lists reports coverage, so the meaningful signal is where tiles exist at all: cellular infrastructure was already thin in the epicenter before the flood degraded it further.

Covered-tile density (light dots) under the population layer
7,949 covered tiles logged corridor-wideSparser dot field = thinner baseline cellular footprint

Covered tiles per 100 km²

Rasuwa sits at roughly a fifth the tile density of Kathmandu Valley or Nuwakot — the least-connected zone on the corridor is also the one now hardest to reach by road.

Movement anomalies

Meta MOV · origin–destination flows, 08:00 & 16:00 NPT snapshots

Arcs show tile-to-tile movement whose 26 Aug volume deviated most from baseline (z-score, capped at ±4). Rasuwa and Dhading are almost absent from the scored-flow set — too few devices there clear Meta's privacy threshold — so the strongest visible signal sits one tier downstream, on the Kathmandu Valley ↔ Nuwakot corridor: the main access route to the disaster zone.

Patterns across the three datasets

Where POP, NET and MOV agree — and where they can't see
Data gap ≠ no impact

The epicenter is where all three signals go dark together

Rasuwa has the sparsest NET footprint on the corridor, the most extreme POP swings (down to –99%, many tiles not reporting at all), and is nearly absent from the scored MOV set. That's one cause — thin, now-degraded infrastructure — suppressing three separate products in exactly the place ground truth matters most.

Downstream agreement

Nuwakot shows a real, moderate outflow signal

POP for Nuwakot declines steadily through the day (–1.2% → –4.1%) while MOV shows elevated two-way traffic with Kathmandu Valley. Read together: a district simultaneously losing resident population and carrying transit/rescue traffic on the main access road.

Plausible destinations

Population gains cluster exactly where you'd expect evacuees to land

Kathmandu Valley, Chitwan (Bharatpur), Gorkha and Tanahu — all named in the ReliefWeb casualty list — show net inbound mobile-population signal (+3.8% to +17%). Consistent with displacement, relief staging and hospital transfers, but not distinguishable from ordinary weekday mobility without ground validation.

Cross-reference with Copernicus

EMSR927's four AOIs line up with the Meta data

Syaprubesi and Timure sit inside the Rasuwa signal-dead-zone (rapid mapping still "ongoing," 0–1 products delivered so far). Bharatpur (Chitwan) sits inside the POP surge zone — the satellite damage-assessment footprint and the mobile-signal inbound anomaly point at the same place.

Methodology & caveats — read before acting on this
  • Mobile signal ≠ census population. Meta's POP/MOV figures are baseline-normalized counts of detected mobile devices/app users, not verified headcounts. Treat every figure here as a proxy, not a survey result.
  • Z-scores are capped at ±4 by Meta's own methodology. Rasuwa's true anomaly magnitude is understated by every chart on this page.
  • Sparse tiles are suppressed, not zeroed. Differential-privacy thresholds mean very low-population or low-signal tiles simply drop out of the data rather than reporting near-zero — this is the main reason the epicenter itself looks emptier in the data than it should.
  • NET predates the flood. The coverage file is timestamped 00:00 NPT, roughly nine hours before the ~09:00 onset. It shows pre-event infrastructure density, not a live outage map. A post-event NET refresh, if released, should supersede the coverage reading here.
  • Zone boundaries are rectangular bounding boxes drawn for rapid triage, not official administrative or CBS boundaries. Tiles near a boundary may be attributed to the wrong district.
  • All ReliefWeb/DFS figures are explicitly provisional and were still rising through the day of writing. The source report itself flags a consolidated displacement/needs total as an unpublished priority information gap.
  • This page is a same-day analyst triage for situational awareness. It is not a substitute for the official Copernicus EMSR927 delineation/grading products (activation ongoing) or verified government damage assessments.
